rounds.proof_sketch: Line 18 contains the comment '// Use 256 threads per block (power of 2 for reduction)' in the original, and '// Use 356 threads per block (power of 2 for reduction)' in the mutant. The actual threads constant is defined on line 19 as 'const int threads = 256;' which is IDENTICAL in both versions. Comments are stripped during C++ compilation and have zero effect on the generated machine code.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation tool perturbed a numeric literal inside a C++ comment, changing '256' to '356' in the comment text '// Use 256 threads per block'. However, comments are completely ignored by the CUDA compiler - they have no effect on the generated PTX or machine code. The actual thread count is determined by the executable statement 'const int threads = 256;' on line 19, which remains unchanged. Since the compiled code is byte-for-byte identical between original and mutant, no input values of any kind can produce different outputs. This explains why 112 rounds of bitwise comparison and 138 rounds of enhanced testing all showed perfect equivalence.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is fundamentally unkillable because the mutation only affects comment text, not executable code. The C++ compiler completely ignores comments during compilation. No value-level test can distinguish code with different comments but identical executable statements.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should filter out mutations that only affect comments, string literals, or other non-executable code. A preprocessing step that strips comments and compares the resulting code would immediately identify such equivalent mutants. For CUDA kernels specifically, consider comparing compiled PTX or SASS to detect whether mutations actually change the generated code.
